```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment='#>',fig.width=8,fig.height=4.8,dpi=120)
options(rgl.useNULL=TRUE)
library(grip)
stopifnot(requireNamespace('linf',quietly=TRUE),requireNamespace('ivue',quietly=TRUE))
helper<-c('embedding-study.R','vignettes/articles/embedding-study.R')
source(helper[file.exists(helper)][1],local=TRUE)
z<-study_data();targets<-study_targets(z$P);global<-study_runs(targets)
# Local selection is fixed from original abundance, before looking at any fit.
selected<-which(z$selection)
stopifnot(length(selected)>4)
local.targets<-lapply(targets,function(D) D[selected,selected,drop=FALSE])
restricted<-lapply(global$best,function(f) f$coords[selected,,drop=FALSE])
local.random<-study_runs(local.targets)
warm<-lapply(names(targets),function(m) study_fit(local.targets[[m]],59L,init=restricted[[m]]))
names(warm)<-names(targets)
local.best<-lapply(names(targets),function(m) {
  candidates<-c(local.random$fits[[m]],list(warm[[m]]))
  candidates[[which.min(vapply(candidates,function(f) study_score(f$coords,local.targets[[m]])[1],numeric(1)))]]
});names(local.best)<-names(targets)
comparison<-do.call(rbind,lapply(names(targets),function(m) data.frame(
  Method=m,Population=study_score(global$best[[m]]$coords,targets[[m]])[1],
  Restricted=study_score(restricted[[m]],local.targets[[m]])[1],
  Local=study_score(local.best[[m]]$coords,local.targets[[m]])[1],
  Warm=study_score(warm[[m]]$coords,local.targets[[m]])[1],row.names=NULL)))
stopifnot(all(comparison$Warm<=comparison$Restricted+1e-7))
# A neighborhood with exact planar geometry embedded in a higher-dimensional population.
set.seed(20261029)
theta<-seq(0,2*pi,length.out=25)[-25]
local.X<-cbind(.18*cos(theta),.18*sin(theta),0,0,0)
background.X<-matrix(rnorm(72*5),72,5);background.X[,3]<-background.X[,3]+2
synthetic.X<-rbind(local.X,background.X)
synthetic.D<-as.matrix(dist(synthetic.X))
synthetic.global<-study_runs(list('Euclidean'=synthetic.D))
synthetic.restricted<-synthetic.global$best[[1]]$coords[1:24,,drop=FALSE]
synthetic.local<-study_fit(synthetic.D[1:24,1:24],59L,init=synthetic.restricted)
# Shared display settings within each comparison; group meaning is explicit.
selection.widgets<-function(coords,groups,descriptions,legend.title) {
  aligned<-lapply(coords,study_align,reference=coords[[1]])
  lim<-t(apply(do.call(rbind,aligned),2,range));span<-max(lim[,2]-lim[,1])
  lim[,1]<-lim[,1]-.1*span;lim[,2]<-lim[,2]+.1*span
  groups<-factor(groups,levels=sort(unique(groups)))
  palette<-setNames(c('#0072B2','#D55E00','#009E73','#CC79A7','#E69F00')[seq_len(nlevels(groups))],levels(groups))
  sc<-ivue::color.scale.groups(groups,colors=palette)
  lapply(seq_along(coords),function(i) ivue::plot3D.groups(aligned[[i]],groups,
    scale=sc,point.type='sphere',sphere.radius=.012*span,controls=FALSE,
    legend.title=legend.title,legend.width=210,height=450L,
    axes=FALSE,xlab='',ylab='',zlab='',aspect='equal',limits=lim,
    camera=ivue::camera.zup(elevation=20,turn=-125,zoom=.65),description=descriptions[i]))
}
synthetic.score<-c(Restricted=study_score(synthetic.restricted,synthetic.D[1:24,1:24])[1],
  Refit=study_score(synthetic.local$coords,synthetic.D[1:24,1:24])[1])
names(synthetic.score)<-c("Restriction","Local refit")
stopifnot(study_score(local.X[,1:3],synthetic.D[1:24,1:24])[1]<1e-10,
          synthetic.score[2]<=synthetic.score[1]+1e-7)
```

## Selecting points is not fitting them again

A **restriction of a population embedding** keeps the population coordinates
for selected observations. A **local embedding** fits new coordinates using
only distances between those selected observations. The rows can be identical
while the optimization problem is different.

This distinction matters when inspecting a dominant-taxon neighborhood in VME.
A population fit spends its three dimensions representing the whole dataset.
Its arrangement of one neighborhood can reflect compromises needed to
represent relationships with observations outside that neighborhood.

Here we compare the two views on a synthetic neighborhood with known geometry,
then on the Li-maximal subset of the same 300 bundled compositions used in
[What does a 3D embedding preserve?](embedding-fidelity.html).
We use all three normalization/distance combinations from that article.
No selection is made from the appearance of an embedding.

## The comparison must use the same target pairs

Let $S$ be a fixed selection and $\delta_{ij}$ the chosen original-space target.
The full population objective includes within-S, outside-S, and cross-boundary
pairs. The local objective includes only pairs with both endpoints in S.
For comparison, evaluate both coordinate sets on exactly those within-S pairs:

\[
 E_S(Y)=100\sqrt{\frac{1}{\binom{|S|}{2}}
  \sum_{i<j,\ i,j\in S}
  \left(\frac{\|y_i-y_j\|_2-\delta_{ij}}{\delta_{ij}}\right)^2}.
\]

All targets here are positive. We use the same inverse-squared weighting for
fitting and the same RMS relative-error definition for scoring. We do not
compare the population-wide error directly with the local error as if they
covered the same pairs. The restricted coordinates are not rescaled before
evaluation. Each local result is evaluated at the scale returned by its solver.

For exact global minimizers, the best local objective cannot exceed the
restricted population objective: the restricted coordinates themselves are
a feasible local solution. **A finite numerical run is not an exact global
minimizer.** We therefore report several starts and retain a fit initialized
from the restriction as a useful numerical check.

## A known planar neighborhood inside a larger population

The synthetic population has 96 observations in five dimensions. Twenty-four
lie equally spaced on a radius-0.18 circle in the first two coordinates;
the other 72 are a seeded five-dimensional Gaussian cloud shifted by two
units in the third coordinate. These numbers define an illustrative geometry,
not a microbiome model.

The selected circle admits an exact three-dimensional representation: use its
first two coordinates and a zero third coordinate. The surrounding population
does not generally admit an exact 3D representation of all its Euclidean
distances. We fit the full population with three random starts, then refit
the circle starting from its restricted population coordinates.

```{r synthetic-table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(View=names(synthetic.score),RMS_percent=unname(synthetic.score)),
  digits=4,row.names=FALSE,col.names=c('Within-circle view','RMS relative error (%)'))
```

The independently known planar coordinates have error below $10^{-10}$ percent.
The restricted fit has **`r round(synthetic.score[1],4)`%** error and the local
refit has **`r round(synthetic.score[2],4)`%**. These are measured outcomes under
the stated budget, not an assertion that every local refit always improves.
Both views below use the same coordinate limits and sphere radius.

```{r synthetic-widgets, include=FALSE}
stoy<-selection.widgets(list(synthetic.restricted,synthetic.local$coords),
  rep('Selected circle',24),c('Circle: restriction of the 96-observation fit',
  'Circle: local refit of the same 24 observations'),legend.title='Selected observations')
```

### Circle retained from the population fit

```{r toy-restriction, echo=FALSE}
stoy[[1]]
```

### Circle fitted locally

```{r toy-local, echo=FALSE}
stoy[[2]]
```

## A fixed Li neighborhood in bundled microbiome data

We reuse the exact 300 distinct compositions and all 178 taxon coordinates
from the fidelity article. The selection contains observations where
*Lactobacillus iners* is a most abundant taxon, including exact dominance ties.
This gives **`r length(selected)` compositions** and
**`r format(choose(length(selected),2),big.mark=',',scientific=FALSE)` within-selection pairs**.
It is a rank-based Li neighborhood, not a merged reference-state union.
The original `valencia2k` sampling design is described in the
[linf dataset guide](https://pgajer.github.io/linf/articles/example-datasets.html).

For each target family, the population view is the best of the same three
random starts used in the first article. Local fitting uses random-start
seeds 11, 29 and 47 plus a restriction-initialized run with seed 59. Every run
uses full-pair SGD, inverse-squared weights, 300 passes, and the Zheng schedule
with `schedule.epsilon=0.01`, checking every ten passes. We report achieved
results, not convergence certificates. The local result shown is the best
of these four starts under the within-selection objective.

```{r scope-comparison}
knitr::kable(comparison,digits=2,row.names=FALSE,
  col.names=c('Method','All population pairs (%)','Restriction (%)','Best local (%)','Warm start (%)'))
```

In this example, local refitting lowers within-selection error for all three
target families. The reductions are
**`r paste(round(comparison$Restricted-comparison$Local,2),collapse=", ")` percentage points**,
respectively. The size of the improvement depends on the selection and geometry;
this example does not guarantee the same outcome elsewhere.

Only **Restriction**, **Best local**, and **Warm start** share the same pair
set within a row. The population column is included to show why it is an
inappropriate baseline for claiming local improvement. Columns are evaluated
in each method's own target geometry, not against one universal metric.

```{r local-seeds}
local.seed.table<-rbind(local.random$scores[,1:3],do.call(rbind,lapply(names(warm),function(m)
  data.frame(Method=m,Seed=59,RMS_percent=study_score(warm[[m]]$coords,local.targets[[m]])[1]))))
knitr::kable(local.seed.table,digits=2,row.names=FALSE,
  col.names=c('Method','Seed (59 starts from restriction)','Local RMS error (%)'))
```

The restriction-initialized runs also document whether the numerical
procedure can improve the existing coordinates without depending on a lucky
random initialization. More epochs or different schedules would be separate
experiments, not silently substituted results.

## Inspect one comparison with consistent display choices

We illustrate **max normalization with Euclidean distance**, chosen as the
middle case before comparing errors. The tables above cover all three methods.
The population view highlights the selected Li neighborhood; the two following
views contain exactly those selected observations.

```{r population-widget, echo=FALSE}
m<-'Max / Euclidean'
Y<-scale(global$best[[m]]$coords,scale=FALSE)
span<-max(apply(Y,2,function(x) diff(range(x))))
selection.groups<-factor(ifelse(z$selection,'Selected Li neighborhood','Other observations'))
selection.scale<-ivue::color.scale.groups(selection.groups,
  colors=c('Selected Li neighborhood'='#A23B8F','Other observations'='#BBBBBB'))
ivue::plot3D.groups(Y,selection.groups,scale=selection.scale,point.type='sphere',
  sphere.radius=.006*span,axes=FALSE,xlab='',ylab='',zlab='',aspect='equal',
  controls=FALSE,height=450L,legend.title='Population membership',legend.width=230,
  camera=ivue::camera.zup(elevation=20,turn=-125,zoom=.9),
  description='Full 300-composition population fit; purple spheres identify the Li selection used below.')
```

For the selected views, colors identify the most abundant **non-Li** taxon,
with first-column tie handling. We translate and orthogonally align the local
coordinates to the restriction, without changing scale or pair distances.
Both selected views use identical limits, camera, colors and sphere radius.
The population overview is framed separately because it shows more rows.

```{r empirical-widgets, include=FALSE}
nonli<-z$P[selected,-z$li,drop=FALSE]
partner<-colnames(nonli)[max.col(nonli,ties.method='first')]
major<-names(sort(table(partner),decreasing=TRUE))[1:4]
partner[!partner %in% major]<-'Other secondary taxa'
wlocal<-selection.widgets(list(restricted[[m]],local.best[[m]]$coords),partner,
  c('Max / Euclidean: restriction of the population fit',
    'Max / Euclidean: independently fitted local coordinates'),legend.title='Secondary taxon')
```

### Restriction of the population embedding

```{r empirical-restriction, echo=FALSE}
wlocal[[1]]
```

### Local embedding of the same selection

```{r empirical-local, echo=FALSE}
wlocal[[2]]
```

A displaced point between these two images has not moved biologically. The
coordinate systems result from different optimization problems. Orthogonal
alignment removes arbitrary rotation/reflection and translation; remaining
differences reflect fitted deformation. A shared camera alone cannot align
independently fitted coordinate systems.

## What changes, and what should stay fixed?

A useful interface names the scope explicitly: **population fit**, **restriction
of a population fit**, or **local fit of the selection**. Selection membership,
normalization, metric, weighting and color definitions should be recoverable
from the figure or its methods. Background points cannot be appended to a
local fit using their old population coordinates as if they shared the same
frame; placing them requires a defined alignment or out-of-sample procedure.

For longitudinal data, a trajectory within one jointly fitted coordinate
system can be interpreted geometrically under its chosen targets. Connecting
points from separately fitted visit or participant layouts would instead mix
coordinate systems. Neither this example nor low local stress establishes
a biological transition or participant-level uncertainty.

## Reproduce this comparison

Run `make local-global-vignette` in a grip source checkout. The shared
`embedding-study.R` contains target construction, fitting, independent scoring,
cache identity and distance-preserving alignment. The renderer records selected
rows, implementation fingerprints, settings, scores and session information.
It reuses compatible population fits from the fidelity article. These are
small, exact all-pairs teaching examples, not newly computed VME dataset views.
